_comment: TEMPLATE — never loaded. Copy the entries you want into config/mcp.json.
config/mcp.json ships EMPTY on purpose. MCP servers are per-user: they carry your
credentials, your hosts and your tool surface, so this repo declares none of them.
The machinery around them does ship and is worth understanding before you add any:
* settings.hostConfigDiscovery: 'off' — PI will NOT pick up MCP servers from other
agents' config files on this machine. Everything you get is what is written here.
* settings.directTools: false — an MCP server's tools are reached through a single
namespaced entry point rather than being flattened into the top-level tool list.
Set 'directTools': true per server for the few whose tools you use constantly.
* A server defined by a PROJECT (.pi/mcp.json inside a repo you opened) is denied by
default and must be approved once, per project. See the trust gate in the docs.
* 'command': 'mcp-stdio-guard' wraps a stdio server so it starts from an EMPTY
environment plus an explicit allowlist, instead of inheriting every API key you
have exported. Use it for anything you did not write yourself. Widen the allowlist
with MCP_STDIO_EXTRA_ENV, as the playwright entry below does.
* 'lifecycle': 'lazy' starts the server on first use instead of at session start.
* A server behind a token puts a REFERENCE in 'headers', never the token itself:
'Authorization': 'Bearer ${SOME_TOKEN}'. The variable is expanded at connect time, so the
secret lives in your environment and the config file stays publishable.
Two browser servers, split by OUTPUT rather than by capability. 'lightpanda' is real V8 with no
rendering: it answers text questions ('goto', then 'markdown'/'tree'/'links'/'extract') and can
never produce a screenshot, because it draws nothing. 'playwright' spawns a Chromium and owns
everything visual. Running only 'playwright' is not wrong, it just makes every JS-for-text page
pay for a browser it does not need. Both are 'lazy', so declaring both costs nothing until a
tool is called. 'lightpanda' needs its own binary on PATH; the installer does not offer it for
that reason, so copy this entry by hand once you have installed it.
The three examples below are public services chosen because they are self-explanatory,
not because you need them.
